newsitem.title: USA: Key issues remain unsettled in U.S., EU meat talks.
newsitem.headline: Key issues remain unsettled in U.S., EU meat talks.

text.p: As American and European officials neared the end of another round of talks on a nasty dispute over meat imports Thursday, it appeared that key sticking points remained despite more than 16 hours of negotiatons.
"The big issues are still there ... poultry is still undecided," said European Union spokeswoman Ella Krucoff.
"There's been no agreement, but we're continuing to talk," said Paul Drazek, head U.S. negotiator at the talks and senior trade adviser to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.
Drazek tried to shed a positive light on the talks, and said this week's meetings have been "productive" even if they have not yielded an agreement.
"We went through the remaining issues at some length ... we had, I think, a productive meeting," he said.

Negotiators were scheduled to meet briefly Thursday. The EU team, which had been scheduled to leave in the afternoon, postponed its departure for at least a day. There was talk that the meetings would be continued next week in Europe.

U.S. and EU officials have been meeting this week in a last-ditch effort to resolve a fight over meat import inspection regulations that threatens to disrupt the trade of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of poultry and meat shipments.

Officials have been trying to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks by April 15 when Washington has said it will remove over 100 poultry and meat processing plants from its list of approved exporters.
On April 1, the European Union adopted new rules that halted the shipment of U.S. poultry to Europe, prompting the United States to also implement new requirements for imports.
One of the biggest bones of contention has been over decontamination procedures used by U.S. and EU poultry plants.

The U.S. industry decontaminates products by dipping or rinsing poultry carcasses in a solution containing bacteria-fighting agents, often chlorine. The EU has questioned the use of chlorine, although U.S. industry sources note that chlorination is used by some EU member nations.

The dispute threatens to halt the trade of up to $100 million worth of U.S. poultry and dairy exports to Europe and some $300 million worth of EU meat imports to the United States, mostly pork products from Denmark and Italian hams.
U.S. meat and poultry industry officials have supported the administration's hardline approach in this latest round of negotiations in the years-old dispute.
The hope has been that pushing the issue to the point of a major trade disruption would give negotiators more cause to settle the issue.

"Being faced with certain repercussions always brings a little clarity of focus to the negotiation process and adds incentive on both sides to work out a deal," said an official with the National Cattlemen's Beef Association.
